newsitem.title: UK: German economy seen overriding EMU-effect on mark.
newsitem.headline: German economy seen overriding EMU-effect on mark.

text.p: The mark's recent recovery on the foreign exchanges has been driven by a seemingly contradictory mix of politics and economics but analysts see the latter holding sway in the near-term at least.

On the economics front, recent reports suggest the clouds of gloom hanging over Germany's economy are slowly dissipating. Some argue this will draw a line under current German interest rate levels and act as a boon to the mark.
But confusion about the timetable for European monetary union (EMU) means this argument is no longer black and white.
An economic improvement in Germany would also be seen as raising its chances of satisfying the entry criteria for EMU - a perception which traditionally erodes mark strength.
Analysts said the interest rate impact of German growth is likely to dominate in the short term, however with the EMU effect locking in again later in the year.

"We've already seen the mark weaken this year so far on the back of a perception that the German economy was not showing any signs of strong growth and I think that relationship is likely to continue," said Robert Hayward, economist at Bank of America in London.
Despite record German unemployment levels in January and February, the most recent indicators of business confidence have shown a marked upturn.
The Ifo research institute's survey of west German business sentiment showed a reading of -7.9 in February compared with -13.3 in December and -20.7 this time last year.
Yet Hayward at Bank of America acknowledged the contradiction in much of the currency market's rationale.
There is a view in the market that "anything which is good for the German economy is good for the European economy and is therefore good for monetary union," he said.

This is partly because of recent speculation that weakness in the German economy will make it more difficult for Germany to reach the budget deficit targets necessary to start EMU on time and, therefore, the whole project could be delayed.
A delay of EMU would be seen as positive for the mark because investors would typically demand German securities as a haven from ensuing volatility elsewhere on the continent.
Yet some economists said it was the form of the fledgling EMU and not its launch that was cause for debate.

"It's most likely that we're going to get EMU...and what really matters is the shape of EMU," said Marian Bell, treasury economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland. "I think it'll be a narrow, fairly hard currency bloc."
While this could affect the mark in the longer-term, it was more likely to feel immediate benefits from the growing optimism over the German economy.
"I also don't think the Bundesbank would be happy with a deutschemark weaker than this" given the pick up in the economy, Bell said.

The debate about Germany's eligibility for EMU in 1999 hinges on whether the economy can grow fast enough this year to generate sufficient tax revenue and cut social security payments in order to meet the EU's budgetary rules.

The Maastricht Treaty says the target for budget deficit should be three percent of a country's annual output, but says "special circumstances" can be taken into account if a country is seen to be approaching this level in a sustainable way.
European Union states will be judged on their ability to take part in monetary union on the basis of 1997 data.
